ui.faqIntro: Straight answers about travelling with KiwiCamping.
ui.faq1a: KiwiCamping is an iPhone app for finding places to camp and stay around New Zealand. It bundles a directory of 6,500+ places so the details stay readable without reception, and it turns the ones you save into a road trip with an ordered route, dates, notes and to-dos.
ui.faq2a: More than 6,500 places: DOC campsites, backcountry huts, holiday parks and other bookable stays, freedom camping areas, public dump stations and day-use places across both islands.
ui.faq3a: The place directory is bundled with the app, so names, categories, descriptions, fees, facilities and conditions stay readable well beyond signal. Live services such as weather, routing, Street View, photos and provider pages still need a connection.
ui.faq4q: Can I plan a multi-stop road trip?
ui.faq4a: Yes, and it is the app's main feature. Add places as stops, drag them into order, attach a date and arrival notes to each one, see the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip, open directions to the next stop, check the weather at each one, tick stops off as visited and keep the packing list beside the itinerary. Itinerary details can sync to Calendar.
ui.faq5a: Two kinds. Smart collections (Liked, Starred, Want to visit, Visited, Pins and All saved) fill themselves as you mark places. On top of those you can create your own named collections with an icon and notes for a region, a season, a vehicle or a shortlist.
ui.faq6q: Can I filter for free camps or self-contained sites?
ui.faq6a: Yes, and combinations of them. Filters cover place type, fee, minimum rating, online booking, region and detailed facility and access features, so “free camping areas with toilets and drinking water near Queenstown” is a single query.
ui.faq7q: What is on a place screen?
ui.faq7a: Photos, a description, opening hours, fees, terms and conditions, facilities grouped by type, current alerts, ratings, contact and booking details, weather, Street View where coverage exists, directions, and nearby alternatives.
ui.faq8a: A standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which you can tilt and rotate for real 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, gives the street-level view from the place screen.
ui.faq9q: Can I see prices in my own currency?
ui.faq9a: Yes. Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate, and reported costs are shown in that currency alongside the New Zealand dollar figure.
ui.faq10q: Can I book a campsite in KiwiCamping?
ui.faq10a: Open the booking details for a place to reach its provider and check live availability, prices and terms.
ui.faq11q: Are camping rules the same across New Zealand?
ui.faq11a: No. National law, council bylaws, conservation rules and individual site conditions can all apply. Always follow current signs, land-manager directions, fire restrictions and official alerts.

ui.review1Title: Made our South Island route so much easier
ui.review1Quote: We used it for campsites and holiday parks between Christchurch and Queenstown and honestly it saved us hours. The offline stuff was the big one once we left the main roads... no signal for ages out there.
ui.review2Quote: Quick to browse, easy to filter. Way better than the twelve browser tabs I had going before.
ui.review3Quote: The hut info and the access notes saved us so much planning time. It genuinely feels like it was made by someone who has actually driven around New Zealand rather than someone who read about it. We used it every single day for three weeks and I'd pay double.
ui.review4Title: found a quiet spot after a long drive!
ui.review4Quote: after 6 hours driving we just needed somewhere quiet with a toilet and it took about 2 minutes to find one. much less stressful than guessing from a pin on google maps
ui.review5Quote: Simple and clear. We mixed paid sites and free camping on our first trip and kept coming back to it.
ui.review6Quote: Camped here my whole life and still found spots I didn't know about, which was a bit humbling to be honest. The dump station and water filters are the ones I open most.
ui.review7Quote: Working out which sites actually needed certification used to take me forever, always second guessing whether we'd get a ticket. Having it separated out properly meant we just stopped worrying about it.
ui.review8Title: Worked with no signal on the west coast
ui.review8Quote: Westport down to the glaciers, basically no reception the whole way. Being able to open a site and still read everything made a real difference. That's the whole reason I keep it.
ui.review9Quote: Six people, two vans, nobody had to ask where we were staying next. Reordering everything when the weather turned was easy which I did not expect.

support.title: How can we help?
support.lede: Clear answers for maps, saved places, trip planning and the road ahead.

sections.heading: Finding places
paragraphs: Search by place name, address or description. Move the map and choose the current-area option to focus results around the visible region.
Filter by place type, fee, minimum rating, online booking, region and detailed facility and access features. Combine only the filters that matter so useful alternatives remain visible.
Facilities, fees, access and management can change. Follow current signs and the land manager, then send a correction so the directory can improve.

sections.heading: Saved places
paragraphs: Liked, Visited, Want to Visit and Starred update automatically when you mark places. Pins and All Saved provide other quick views.
Create named collections with an icon and notes, then add any place. Use them for a region, season, vehicle or shortlist.
The app supports private iCloud sync for saved states, collections and trip data when iCloud is available and enabled.

sections.heading: Trip planner
paragraphs: Create a trip, add places and drag them into order. Each stop can carry its own arrival date, notes, weather and visited status, and the planner shows the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip.
Road routing depends on available MapKit directions. The planner retains the stops if a leg fails, but you must confirm current road access yourself.
Start with a camping essentials preset or make your own tasks. Trip progress keeps the list beside the itinerary, and itinerary details can sync to Calendar.

sections.heading: Maps, weather and live details
paragraphs: Switch between the standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which tilts and rotates into 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, opens from the place screen where coverage exists.
Current and forecast weather requires live data. Save critical forecasts and official warnings before leaving coverage.
The bundled place directory keeps core place details available beyond reliable signal. Live maps, routing, weather, photos and external provider pages may require reception.

sections.heading: Prices and currency
paragraphs: Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate. Reported costs are then shown in that currency alongside the New Zealand dollar figure, which helps when you are visiting and not fluent in NZD.
Open a place's booking or contact details to check availability, price and terms with the provider. Prices in the app are reported figures, not live quotes.

sections.heading: Premium and purchases
paragraphs: Map and place details are free, together with two saved lists.
Premium adds unlimited saved lists, trip planning, advanced filters, place weather and road trip routes.
Use Restore Purchases on the Premium screen while signed into the Apple account used for the original transaction.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.lede: KiwiCamping helps you plan a trip without turning your journey into an advertising profile.

sections.heading: Information stored on your device
paragraphs: Saved places, collection membership, trips, notes, checklist items and preferences are stored for the app to work. Location can be used to show your position and nearby places after you grant permission.

sections.heading: iCloud
paragraphs: When iCloud is available and enabled, the app can use your private iCloud database to sync saved states, collections and app records across your devices. Apple provides the underlying service and applies its own terms.

sections.heading: Live Apple services
paragraphs: Map display, directions, Look Around, weather, calendar integration and widgets may use Apple frameworks. Requests and data handling for those services are governed by Apple. Calendar access occurs only after permission and is used to add trip itinerary information you request.

sections.heading: External links and website logs
paragraphs: Place details can open booking providers, websites, social profiles, phone numbers, email addresses and map apps. Those services receive information according to their own policies when you choose to open them.

Hosting providers may process routine technical logs such as IP address, browser type and requested URL for delivery, reliability and security. KiwiCamping does not use advertising trackers on this website.

sections.heading: Website analytics
paragraphs: This website uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits and to see which pages lead people to the App Store. Google processes this data on our behalf as a processor. For visitors in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland the service is provided by Google Ireland Limited, and elsewhere by Google LLC.

Analytics records the pages you view, your device, browser and screen type, an approximate location derived from your IP address (Google does not store the address itself), the page that sent you here and your clicks on App Store links. It never receives your name, your email address or anything you save in the app.

When analytics is allowed, Google Analytics sets two first-party cookies: _ga, and a second whose name starts with _ga_. Both expire after 13 months. In the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland these cookies are set only after you choose Accept on the consent bar. Until then, and if you choose Decline, no analytics cookies are stored and Google receives only cookieless signals that carry no identifier. You can change your choice at any time with the Privacy choices link at the foot of every page.

Google signals and ad personalisation are switched off, so analytics data is not linked to Google accounts and is not used for advertising. Analytics data is kept for 14 months and then deleted. KiwiCamping still uses no advertising trackers on this website.

sections.heading: Retention and control
paragraphs: You can delete app records through the app and manage iCloud data through your Apple account. Removing the app can remove local data, while synced copies may remain in iCloud until separately deleted.

sections.heading: Children and contact
paragraphs: KiwiCamping is a general travel utility and is not directed to children. Do not submit personal information about a child through support.
For privacy questions, contact KiwiCamping support.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.lede: KiwiCamping is a planning aid. It does not replace official signs, land-manager directions, emergency warnings, road advice or your responsibility to travel within your capability.

sections.heading: Travel information changes
paragraphs: Places, prices, access, facilities, phone coverage, weather, fire conditions, roads and booking arrangements can change without notice. Verify critical details with the responsible authority or provider before travel and again close to departure.

sections.heading: No booking or access guarantee
paragraphs: A listing does not guarantee that a place is open, legal for your setup, reachable by your vehicle or available. External booking and contact links are provided for convenience. Contracts are between you and the third-party provider.

sections.heading: Safety and lawful use
paragraphs: You must obey signs, permits, closures, fire restrictions, road rules and directions from rangers, iwi, hapū, emergency services and land managers. Do not use the app while driving.

sections.heading: User data
paragraphs: You are responsible for notes, trip plans and other information you save. Keep separate copies of permits, bookings and safety-critical plans when loss of access could put a trip at risk.

sections.heading: Purchases
paragraphs: Any in-app purchase is processed by Apple and subject to the terms shown at purchase. Features, packaging and prices may change where allowed. Use Apple’s purchase tools for billing, cancellation and refund matters.

sections.heading: Intellectual property and contact
paragraphs: KiwiCamping branding, interface and original editorial content belong to their respective owner. Place names and public facts remain the property or responsibility of their original sources.
Questions can be sent to KiwiCamping support.

index.metaTitle: NZ Road Trip Calculators: Fuel, Driving Time, Campsite Costs
index.metaDescription: Free New Zealand road trip calculators: fuel cost, driving time by road type, campsite cost per person or per site, NZD currency conversion and campervan water tanks.
index.toolsText: Each calculator has its own page with the formula, a worked example using New Zealand figures, the assumptions behind it and answers to common questions.

fuel.metaTitle: Fuel Cost Calculator NZ: Campervan Road Trip Fuel
fuel.metaDescription: Work out litres and fuel cost for a New Zealand road trip from distance, L/100 km and the pump price, with the formula, a 1,000 km worked example and MBIE's benchmark.
fuel.h1: Fuel cost calculator for a New Zealand road trip
fuel.intro: Enter the route distance, your vehicle's loaded fuel use and the price per litre. The default price is MBIE's national board price for regular 91 petrol in the week ending 26 July 2026.
fuel.cardText: Enter the full route distance, the vehicle's loaded fuel use and the expected price per litre. Remote prices can exceed city benchmarks.
fuel.formulaNote: Consumption is quoted per 100 kilometres, so dividing by 100 turns it into litres per kilometre. The sum is linear: double the distance and both the litres and the cost double.
fuel.example: A {distance} km route in a campervan using {consumption} L/100 km needs {litres} litres of fuel. At {price} a litre, that is {cost}.
assumptions: The default price is a national benchmark. Remote stations, including on the West Coast and in Fiordland, often charge more, so fill up before long gaps between towns.
Use the loaded consumption of the vehicle you are actually driving. A full campervan on hills and into a headwind uses more than its brochure figure.
Add the local driving around each stop. Supermarket runs, viewpoints and side roads add up over a long route.
Diesel vehicles pay road user charges (RUC) for every 1,000 km on top of fuel. This calculator covers fuel only.
faq: How much fuel does a campervan use in New Zealand?

It depends on the vehicle, the load and the roads. Use the figure from your hire company or vehicle and allow a margin for hills. The 12 L/100 km default is a planning figure for a loaded campervan, not a measured average.
Does the fuel cost include road user charges?
No. Diesel vehicles in New Zealand pay road user charges per 1,000 km separately from fuel. Ask your hire company whether RUC is included in the rate, and check NZTA for current charges.
Where does the default fuel price come from?
It is MBIE's national board price for regular 91 petrol in the week ending 26 July 2026. MBIE publishes fuel prices every week, so check the latest figure before you go.

drive.metaTitle: Driving Time Calculator NZ: Realistic Hours by Road Type
drive.metaDescription: Estimate how long a New Zealand driving day really takes from the distance, the kind of road and your stops, with the formula, a worked example and the speeds used.
drive.h1: Driving time calculator for New Zealand roads
drive.intro: Routing apps give moving time on an ideal road. This calculator takes the distance you already know, an average speed for the kind of road and 20 minutes for every stop, which is where a New Zealand driving day usually runs over.
drive.cardTitle: How long that day really takes.
drive.cardText: Routing apps give moving time on an ideal road. This adds the road character and your actual stops, which is where a day usually runs over.
drive.formulaNote: The average speed is not the speed limit. It allows for corners, hills, one-lane bridges, towns and slower traffic. The four road types use 85, 70, 60 and 45 km/h.
drive.example: A {distance} km day on winding or coastal roads at {speed} km/h is {driving} of driving. Add {stops} stops at 20 minutes each and the day takes {total}.
assumptions: The average speeds are planning figures for a car or campervan in good conditions, not measured averages for any one road.
Each stop counts 20 minutes for fuel, food, a toilet or a viewpoint. Ferries, road works and long walks need adding on top.
Weather, slips and closures change routes. Check NZTA's journey planner for current road conditions before you set off.
faq: How far can you drive in a day in New Zealand?

There is no single number. Winding roads, one-lane bridges and stops keep average speeds well below the open-road limit, so a day that looks short on a map can take most of the daylight. Enter the distance and road type to see the hours, and plan regular rest breaks.
Why is this longer than my maps app?
Maps apps estimate moving time with no stops. This uses an average for the kind of road and adds time for each stop, which is closer to how a camping day actually goes.
Does it work for a campervan?
Yes. Choose a slower road type if you are driving a large vehicle, towing, or new to driving on the left.

campsite.metaTitle: Campsite Cost Calculator NZ: Per Person or Per Site?
campsite.metaDescription: Compare a DOC campsite charged per adult with a holiday park charged per site for your group and nights, with the formula, a worked example and DOC fee figures from the data.
campsite.h1: Campsite cost calculator: per person or per site
campsite.intro: DOC campsites charge per adult per night, while a holiday park usually charges per site. Which one is cheaper flips with the size of your group, and this works it out for your nights.
campsite.cardText: A DOC campsite usually charges per adult and a holiday park usually charges per site. The cheaper option flips with party size, which catches families out.
formula: Per-adult total = adults × nights × rate per adult
Per-site total = nights × rate per site
The lower total is the cheaper option for your group
campsite.formulaNote: The per-adult total grows with every extra adult, while the per-site total does not. That is why the answer changes between a couple and a family.
campsite.example: {adults} adults staying {nights} nights at {rateAdult} per adult pay {totalAdult}. The same stay at {rateSite} per site costs {totalSite}, so {verdict}.
assumptions: Children are left out. Many DOC campsites charge a reduced rate for ages 5 to 17 and nothing for infants, and holiday parks set their own child rates.
The default rates are examples, not quotes. In the DOC data as of {docDate}, {docFree} DOC campsites are free, and the lowest adult rate listed at paid ones runs from {docMin} to {docMax} per night.
Holiday parks set their own prices, which change with the season, power and site size. Check the park before you book.
faq: How much does a campsite cost per night in New Zealand?

DOC campsites are either free or charge per adult. In the DOC data as of {docDate}, the lowest adult rate at paid DOC campsites runs from {docMin} to {docMax} per night, with a median of {docMedian}. Holiday parks set their own site prices, so compare the total for your group.
Is per person or per site cheaper for a family?
Per site usually wins as the group grows, because the site price stays the same while per-adult charges multiply. Enter your own rates to see where the break-even point falls.
Do children pay at DOC campsites?
At many DOC campsites children aged 5 to 17 pay a reduced rate and infants stay free. The fee for each campsite is on its DOC page.

currency.metaTitle: NZD Currency Converter: New Zealand Prices in 9 Currencies
currency.metaDescription: Convert New Zealand dollar prices to and from USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, JPY, CNY, KRW, INR and SGD using Reserve Bank of New Zealand reference rates.
currency.h1: NZD currency converter for New Zealand trip prices
currency.intro: Convert a New Zealand price into your own currency, or your currency into New Zealand dollars, using Reserve Bank of New Zealand reference rates from {rateDate}.
currency.cardText: Reference conversion for trip planning using Reserve Bank of New Zealand rates from {rateDate}. Your bank or card may use another rate and add fees.
formula: Amount in NZD = amount ÷ rate of the currency you convert from
Result = amount in NZD × rate of the currency you convert to
currency.formulaNote: Each rate is the number of units of that currency per 1 New Zealand dollar, so every conversion passes through NZD.
currency.example: {amount} at {rate} US dollars per New Zealand dollar is {converted}.
assumptions: These are reference rates from {rateDate}. Exchange rates move every day.
Banks, cards and cash machines use their own rates and may add fees, so the amount you pay can differ.
Japanese yen and Korean won are shown without decimals.
faq: What currency is used in New Zealand?
The New Zealand dollar (NZD). Prices in shops, campsites and holiday parks are quoted in NZD.
Is this the rate my bank will give me?
Probably not exactly. This uses reference rates from {rateDate}. Your bank or card provider applies its own rate and fees, so treat the result as a planning figure.

water.metaTitle: Campervan Water Tank Calculator: Fresh and Grey Water Days
water.metaDescription: Work out how many days a campervan's fresh and grey water tanks last for your group, with the formula, a worked example and the daily figures behind it.
water.intro: A tank size in litres only becomes useful once it is days. Enter the fresh and grey water capacity and the number of people to see which tank sets your limit.
water.cardText: Capacity in litres only becomes useful once it is expressed in days. Fresh and grey water are shown separately, because whichever runs out first sets the limit.
formula: Fresh water days = fresh tank (L) ÷ (people × 11 L a day)
Grey water days = grey tank (L) ÷ (people × 9 L a day)
The lower of the two is how long you can stay before refilling or emptying
water.formulaNote: Grey water is the waste from sinks and showers. It is lower than fresh water use because drinking water and cooking water do not all end up in the tank.
water.example: {people} people with a {freshTank} litre fresh tank and a {greyTank} litre grey tank have {freshDays} days of fresh water and {greyDays} days of grey water, so the fresh tank sets the limit.
assumptions: 11 litres of fresh water and 9 litres of grey water per person per day are planning figures for careful use: drinking, cooking, washing up and a quick wash. Showers use far more.
Toilet cassettes and black water are not included.
Empty grey water only at a dump station. Never on the ground or into a stormwater drain.
faq: How long does 100 litres of fresh water last in a campervan?
For two careful users at 11 litres each a day, about four and a half days. Showers and washing clothes shorten that a lot.
Where can I empty grey water in New Zealand?
At a dump station. Many holiday parks have one, and councils run public ones in many towns. Never empty grey water onto the ground or into a stormwater drain.
Which tank runs out first?
Whichever is smaller for your use. Grey tanks are often smaller than fresh tanks, so check both rather than only the fresh water gauge.

coromandel-rotorua-road-trip.title: Auckland, Coromandel and Rotorua: a 5-day camping loop
coromandel-rotorua-road-trip.description: Pacific beaches, forest roads and geothermal country on a compact North Island circuit.
coromandel-rotorua-road-trip.imageAlt: Coromandel coast seen from a winding road
coromandel-rotorua-road-trip.intro: Five days is enough to connect the Coromandel Peninsula with Rotorua when the first and last drives stay disciplined. The reward is a route that moves from salt air to native forest and geothermal steam without wasting a day in transit.

sections.heading: Day 1 and 2: into the Coromandel
body: Leave Auckland outside commuter traffic and use Thames to buy food and fuel before the coast road narrows. The western side is beautiful but slower than the distance suggests, especially for a tall campervan.
Spend the second day around Whangamatā, Hot Water Beach or Cathedral Cove according to current access. Choose a legal campground near the activity rather than crossing the peninsula after sunset.

sections.heading: Day 3: cross to the forest
body: Use Whitianga or Coromandel Town for a proper reset before the inland drive. Kauaeranga Valley camps suit travellers ready for simpler facilities, while holiday parks offer showers, power and an easier wet-weather night.
The peninsula receives heavy rain and slips can affect local roads. Check Waka Kotahi and council updates before committing to a remote approach, then keep a sealed-road alternative saved.

sections.heading: Day 4 and 5: Rotorua and return
body: Rotorua needs a full day for geothermal walks, lakes and cultural experiences. Stay in an authorised campground or holiday park and treat geothermal fences and warning signs as firm boundaries.
Return to Auckland through Waikato or continue south if this loop opens a longer trip. Do not pair a late thermal-pool session with a tired drive through unfamiliar rural roads.

sections.heading: Roads that take longer than the map says
body: The 309 Road across the Coromandel range is unsealed in part and slow, and the coastal route between Thames and Coromandel Town is a narrow shelf road with almost no passing opportunity. Neither is difficult, but both run well over the time a routing app suggests, particularly in a large vehicle.

Allow a full unhurried day for the peninsula rather than treating it as a transit. The reward is the beaches on the east side, and rushing past them to reach Rotorua on schedule removes the point of the loop.
tips: 309 Road is partly unsealed
Thames to Coromandel is narrow and slow
Give the peninsula a whole day

sections.heading: Cathedral Cove and Hot Water Beach need timing
body: Hot Water Beach only works around two hours either side of low tide, and the tide table decides your day rather than your itinerary. Check it before you set the order of stops, because arriving at high tide means there is genuinely nothing to do there.

Cathedral Cove access has changed repeatedly after storm damage and slips, and the walking route and parking arrangements have been altered more than once. Check the current DOC status rather than an older blog, and consider the water taxi from Hahei if the track is restricted.

sections.heading: Booking the summer beaches
body: Between Christmas and late January the east coast campgrounds at Hahei, Hot Water Beach and Ōpoutere fill completely, often booked months ahead. Arriving without a reservation in that window is not a plan, and the freedom camping options on the peninsula are limited and heavily patrolled.
Outside that window the same sites have space a few days out and cost less. If your dates are flexible at all, February and March give you the same beaches without the queue.
tips: Peak beaches book months ahead
Freedom camping is limited here
February and March are far easier

sections.heading: Rotorua earns a slower stop
body: The geothermal parks, the redwoods and the lake all deserve more than an afternoon, and the holiday parks here are genuinely convenient with the added novelty of thermally heated pools. It is a good place to spend two nights rather than one, particularly if the Coromandel weather has been wet.
The sulphur smell is real and fades from your awareness within a few hours. What does not fade is the effect on silver jewellery, so leave anything precious packed for the stay.

sections.heading: Choosing where to base each night
body: Thames works as a first night if you leave Auckland late, but it is a service town rather than a destination and the peninsula proper starts north of it. Whitianga and Hahei are the natural east coast bases, with Hahei closest to the walks and Whitianga carrying more services and a wider choice of campgrounds.

On the Rotorua leg, the lakeside holiday parks put you close to the geothermal parks and the redwoods without needing to drive back into town each morning. Blue Lake and Lake Ōkāreka are quieter than the central options and only a short drive from the attractions.
If the weather turns on the peninsula, the sensible move is to cut a beach day and arrive in Rotorua early. Almost everything there works in rain, which is rarely true of the Coromandel coast.

sections.heading: Getting out of Auckland
body: Leaving Auckland southbound on a Friday afternoon or returning on a Sunday evening adds a long time to the drive. Aim to travel against the flow, or leave early enough that the motorway is still moving.
The Hauraki Rail Trail out of Thames is a flat cycle route through the plains and gorge, and bike hire is easy. It works well as a rest day if the peninsula weather is poor.
tips: Avoid Friday and Sunday motorway peaks
Hauraki Rail Trail is a good wet-day option

northland-cape-reinga-camping-route.title: Northland to Cape Reinga: a 7-day camping route
northland-cape-reinga-camping-route.description: Harbours, kauri forest and long northern beaches on the road to Te Rerenga Wairua.
northland-cape-reinga-camping-route.intro: The road north is not only a dash to the lighthouse. A week allows time for the Bay of Islands, west-coast forest and the cultural weight of Te Rerenga Wairua, with nights placed where services naturally thin out.

sections.heading: Whangārei to the Bay of Islands
body: Break the first leg around Whangārei Heads or Tutukaka before reaching Paihia. Holiday parks are convenient around the bay, while smaller coastal camps need closer checks for access, water and booking rules.

Use the passenger ferry to Russell rather than shifting the vehicle for every outing. Waitangi Treaty Grounds deserves unhurried time and should be approached as a living historic place, not a quick photo stop.

sections.heading: Across to the west coast
body: Travel through Kerikeri and Kāeo toward Ahipara, or cross to Waipoua Forest if the route and conditions allow. Follow every kauri hygiene station and keep footwear free of soil between forest walks.

Ninety Mile Beach is officially a road, but it is not an ordinary road. Tides, stream entrances, rental exclusions and soft sand make a coach trip or local advice the sensible choice for many visitors.

sections.heading: Cape Reinga and the final night
body: Carry enough fuel for the northern leg and check campsite details before reception disappears. Te Paki and nearby DOC options are exposed, simple and much better approached before dark.
At Cape Reinga, stay on formed paths and respect the significance of the headland to Māori. Leave the return drive for daylight and avoid turning the lighthouse visit into a race back to Auckland.

sections.heading: Ninety Mile Beach is not a road for your vehicle
body: The beach is legally a road, and it is also where a steady stream of rental vehicles are written off every year by incoming tide and soft sand. Almost every rental agreement prohibits it, insurance will not cover the recovery, and a stuck vehicle on a rising tide is lost quickly.
Take a commercial bus tour if you want to travel the beach. They run to tide windows, carry recovery equipment and know the entry points, and it costs a fraction of an excess claim.
tips: Rentals are not covered on the beach
Take the bus tour instead
Tide takes vehicles every year

sections.heading: Fuel and supplies thin out north of Kaitaia
body: Kaitaia is the last town with full services before Cape Reinga, and the stretch beyond it has limited fuel, few shops and patchy reception. Fill up and restock there rather than assuming something will appear, and check opening hours if you are travelling on a Sunday.

The road to the Cape is sealed the whole way now, which surprises people expecting gravel, but it is still a long out-and-back. Budget most of a day for the return trip from a base around Ahipara or Pukenui.

sections.heading: Respect the significance of Te Rerenga Wairua
body: Cape Reinga is one of the most spiritually significant places in the country for Māori, the departure point of spirits on their journey. Food is not permitted at the lighthouse area, and the expectation of quiet respectful behaviour is not a tourism formality.
Read the signage at the car park before walking down. Observing what is asked costs nothing and matters a great deal to the people whose place it is.
tips: No food at the lighthouse area
Read the signage before walking down
Quiet respect is expected

sections.heading: Kauri dieback governs the forest walks
body: Waipoua Forest and the northern kauri stands are managed under strict hygiene controls because kauri dieback is spread by soil on footwear. Use every cleaning station, scrub the soil off properly rather than just spraying, and stay on the boardwalks without exception.

Some tracks are closed permanently to protect stands and will not reopen. Check the current DOC status before planning a walk around a specific tree, because the situation changes and old guidance circulates widely.

sections.heading: Both coasts are worth doing
body: Northland has two very different coastlines and the standard mistake is running north on one and straight back down the same road. The east coast has the sheltered bays, the swimming and most of the towns; the west has Ninety Mile Beach, the giant dunes at Te Paki and the kauri forests.

A clean route runs north up the east coast through Whangārei, Paihia and Matauri Bay, out to the Cape, then south down the west through Ahipara, the Hokianga and Waipoua Forest. It costs no extra driving and gives you two entirely different weeks in one.

Sandboarding at Te Paki is genuinely good fun and boards can be hired at the dunes. Wear something you do not mind ruining, and walk up the firm sand at the edge rather than the middle, which is exhausting.

sections.heading: The Hokianga and the kauri forests
body: The southern half of the west coast route runs through the Hokianga, with the harbour crossing at Rawene by vehicle ferry and the giant dunes at Opononi opposite. It is quieter and more atmospheric than the east coast towns.

Waipoua Forest sits just south of there and holds Tane Mahuta. Allow time for the hygiene stations and note that photography stops and parking are limited, so an early or late visit is considerably better.
tips: Rawene vehicle ferry saves a long drive
Visit Waipoua early or late

bay-of-islands-camping-week.title: A week camping around the Bay of Islands
bay-of-islands-camping-week.description: Island ferries, sheltered coves and historic waterfront towns without changing camp every night.
bay-of-islands-camping-week.imageAlt: Boats in a calm Bay of Islands cove
bay-of-islands-camping-week.intro: The Bay of Islands works best from two bases rather than seven different camps. Keep the vehicle still for a few days, use ferries and boats for the water, then shift north for Kerikeri and the quieter bays.

sections.heading: Choose the first base
body: Paihia keeps ferries, groceries and tours within walking distance, while Russell offers a smaller waterfront atmosphere after the day visitors leave. Confirm parking and late-arrival conditions before choosing between them.

Use the first morning for Waitangi and allow more time than the headline attractions suggest. The grounds, museum and landscape explain far more when the visit is not squeezed between boat departures.

sections.heading: Let the boat replace the road
body: Sailing, kayaking and water taxis reveal why this region is a bay rather than a chain of viewpoints. Check marine weather and operator conditions, then pack sun protection and a warm layer even on a bright morning.
Urupukapuka and other islands have conservation rules that protect wildlife. Clean gear, take rubbish away and use only the campsites and facilities identified for overnight stays.

sections.heading: Kerikeri and the northern bays
body: Move to Kerikeri for food, orchards, historic sites and easier access to Matauri Bay or Whangaroa. Summer bookings and local road traffic can make a spontaneous coastal night difficult.
Leave one day unassigned. Wind may move a boat trip, rain may favour a forest walk, and a flexible plan gives the best bay of the week room to become a second visit.

sections.heading: Getting out on the water is the point
body: The Bay of Islands is a marine destination and a week spent entirely on land misses most of it. Options run from the passenger ferry between Paihia and Russell, which takes minutes and costs little, through to full-day sailing, dolphin and Hole in the Rock trips.
Book weather-dependent trips early in your stay rather than late. That way a cancelled day can be rescheduled within the week instead of becoming the thing you missed.
tips: Book boat trips early in the week
The Russell ferry is cheap and quick
Leave a spare day for weather

sections.heading: Urupukapuka Island camping
body: DOC runs campsites on Urupukapuka, reached by water taxi from Paihia or Russell. It is a genuinely different experience from a mainland holiday park: no vehicles, limited facilities, and you carry everything in and out including your rubbish.

Book the site and the boat together and check the return timetable carefully, because the last taxi is not negotiable. Take more water than you expect to need, since supply on the island is limited and untreated.

sections.heading: Waitangi is worth the entry fee
body: The Waitangi Treaty Grounds are the single most historically important site in the country, and the guided tour and cultural performance are what make the visit land rather than the buildings alone. Allow half a day, and take the guided option rather than wandering it alone.

For a fuller picture, pair it with the Russell museum and Christ Church, which carries musket ball damage from the 1845 fighting. The two sites together explain the region far better than either does on its own.
tips: Take the guided tour, not self-guided
Allow half a day at Waitangi
Pair it with Russell for context

sections.heading: Summer here is genuinely busy
body: January in Paihia and Russell means full campgrounds, booked boat trips and queues for the ferry. It is also warm, calm and exactly when the water is best, so the trade is real rather than one-sided.

Shoulder season in November or March gives you the same coastline with space and lower prices, though the water is cooler and some operators reduce their schedules. Check that the specific trip you want is still running.

sections.heading: Where to stay around the bay
body: Paihia has the most accommodation and the ferry to Russell, which makes it the practical base for a week without a boat. It is also the busiest and noisiest, particularly in January. Russell is quieter and more attractive but has fewer campgrounds and everything runs on the ferry timetable.

Kerikeri sits inland with the historic Stone Store and Kemp House, good food and cheaper sites, and it works well for a couple of nights if you want a break from the waterfront. It is around twenty minutes from Paihia.

For something quieter again, the campgrounds around Matauri Bay and Tauranga Bay north of the Bay of Islands give you comparable coastline with a fraction of the traffic, and they are an easy detour on the way north.

sections.heading: Rainy day options
body: Northland gets substantial rain and a week here will usually include a wet day. The Waitangi Treaty Grounds, the Kerikeri historic buildings and the Kawiti glow worm caves near Waiomio all work regardless of weather.
Boat trips are the thing most likely to be cancelled, which is the argument for booking them early in the week rather than saving them for the end.
tips: Book boat trips early in the week
Waitangi and Kerikeri work in rain

east-cape-road-trip.title: East Cape road trip: Gisborne to Ōpōtiki
east-cape-road-trip.description: A slow coastal circuit through surf towns, pōhutukawa bays and remote eastern roads.
east-cape-road-trip.imageAlt: Remote East Cape road beside the Pacific
east-cape-road-trip.intro: State Highway 35 traces one of the country's most rewarding slow roads. Fuel, opening hours and storm damage matter more here, so the itinerary should follow daylight and local conditions instead of a fixed arrival time.

sections.heading: Gisborne to Tolaga Bay
body: Start with a full tank and groceries in Gisborne, then stop at coastal settlements without assuming every service will be open. Tolaga Bay gives the first night an easy landmark and a chance to walk rather than drive.
Ask permission wherever land or beach access is not clearly public. Marae, urupā and working farms are not informal camping grounds, even when an old online comment suggests otherwise.

sections.heading: Around the cape
body: Tokomaru Bay and Te Araroa reward travellers who stay long enough to notice the communities between viewpoints. Drive conservatively through narrow bends and expect livestock, cyclists and road repairs.
The side trip to the East Cape lighthouse includes a long staircase and remote access. Check the road before setting out and do not count on reception for a last-minute campsite search.

sections.heading: Finish through Waihau Bay
body: Waihau Bay and the coast toward Ōpōtiki provide a gentler final leg when weather is settled. Storms can close or damage the highway, so review council and Waka Kotahi notices each morning.
Reach Ōpōtiki with daylight for fuel, supplies and the next decision. If the road has demanded more concentration than expected, stop there instead of continuing tired toward Tauranga or Rotorua.

sections.heading: This is a route about slowing down
body: State Highway 35 around the Cape is one of the few places left in New Zealand where you can drive for an hour and pass almost nobody. There is no headline attraction, and travellers who arrive looking for one are usually disappointed. The road, the bays and the pace are the point.
Give it three days minimum. Done as a two-day dash between Gisborne and Ōpōtiki it becomes a long drive through places you did not stop at, which is the one way to get this route wrong.
tips: Three days minimum for the Cape
There is no headline attraction
Passing nobody is the appeal

sections.heading: Services and reception are genuinely sparse
body: Fuel is available at intervals but not everywhere, opening hours are short, and card facilities occasionally fail. Carry cash, fill up at Gisborne and Ōpōtiki, and top up whenever you pass a station with more than half a tank showing.
Mobile coverage disappears for long stretches. Download what you need, tell someone your rough plan, and do not count on being able to look something up or call ahead from the road.

sections.heading: You are travelling through iwi land and small communities
body: The Cape is predominantly Māori land and the communities along it are small and close. Freedom camping is restricted in many places and the local expectation of respectful behaviour is high, particularly around marae, urupā and access to beaches.
Ask rather than assume, buy from the local shops, and never camp somewhere simply because nobody appeared to stop you. The welcome here is real and it depends on visitors behaving well.
tips: Ask before camping anywhere unclear
Buy from the local shops
Marae and urupā are not attractions

sections.heading: East Cape Lighthouse and the first sunrise
body: The lighthouse walk is roughly 700 steps from the car park at the end of a gravel road, and the reward is the first place on mainland New Zealand to see the sunrise. It is a genuinely worthwhile early start, particularly around the solstice.
The access road is unsealed and can be rough after rain. Check its condition and your rental agreement before committing, and allow considerably longer than the distance suggests.

sections.heading: What is actually worth stopping for
body: Tolaga Bay wharf is the longest in the country at over 600 metres and worth the walk to the end. Tokomaru Bay has the ruins of the old freezing works and a genuinely good beach. Te Puia Springs and Waipiro Bay are small and quiet in a way that rewards an unplanned stop.

Tikitiki has St Mary's Church, one of the most remarkable interiors in New Zealand, decorated throughout with carving and tukutuku and built as a memorial to Ngāti Porou soldiers. It is unlocked and free and most people drive past it without knowing.

Hicks Bay and Te Araroa mark the northern end, and the pōhutukawa at Te Araroa is claimed to be the largest in the country. From there it is a short run to the lighthouse road and then west towards Ōpōtiki.

sections.heading: Timing and season
body: Summer brings the pohutukawa into flower along the coast, which is the classic image of this route, and the small settlements are busiest over the Christmas period. Outside that the road is close to empty.
Winter is quiet and green but services reduce further and daylight is short for a route where the driving is the point. Autumn is the sweet spot for both weather and space.
tips: Pohutukawa flower in December
Autumn balances weather and quiet

taranaki-forgotten-world-highway.title: Taranaki and the Forgotten World Highway camping loop
taranaki-forgotten-world-highway.description: Black-sand coast, volcanic forest and the remote road between Stratford and Taumarunui.
taranaki-forgotten-world-highway.imageAlt: Mount Taranaki above a rural highway
taranaki-forgotten-world-highway.intro: This loop circles a mountain, then follows State Highway 43 through saddles, farmland and the single-lane Moki Tunnel. Three or four nights creates space for weather around Taranaki and a patient crossing of the Forgotten World Highway.

sections.heading: New Plymouth and the mountain
body: Use New Plymouth as the reliable base for fuel, food and a coastal day. Mountain cloud changes quickly, so walk the lower tracks when visibility or wind makes exposed routes a poor choice.
Egmont National Park trailheads are not interchangeable campsites. Stay only where overnight use is permitted and use the exact access advice for the track and vehicle.

sections.heading: Stratford to Whangamōmona
body: Fill the tank in Stratford and treat the highway as the day's experience. The sealed and unsealed sections, narrow bridges and tight bends suit a calm pace rather than a target arrival time.
Whangamōmona has limited accommodation and camping capacity. Confirm the night in advance, particularly around events, and carry food for hours when small businesses are closed.

sections.heading: Taumarunui and the return
body: The Tangarakau Gorge and Moki Tunnel demand attention from wide or high vehicles. Know the campervan dimensions and stop before any section that does not provide safe clearance.

Taumarunui restores ordinary services and opens routes toward Tongariro or Waikato. Check fatigue before adding another long leg, because the highway's short distance hides a full day of concentration.

sections.heading: The Forgotten World Highway is a commitment
body: State Highway 43 runs roughly 150 kilometres between Stratford and Taumarunui with no fuel along it, a section of unsealed road through the Tangarakau Gorge, and a single-lane tunnel. It takes far longer than the distance implies and there is no way to shortcut out of the middle.
Fill the tank at either end, carry water and food, and check the road status before setting out. It is a fine drive in reasonable weather and an unpleasant one in heavy rain.
tips: No fuel for 150 kilometres
Part unsealed, one single-lane tunnel
Check road status before you start

sections.heading: Whangamōmona is the reason to go slowly
body: The self-declared Republic of Whangamōmona, with its own passports stamped at the hotel, is the highlight of the route and a genuinely good pub stop. The Republic Day celebration runs biennially and fills the village completely, which is either the reason to go or the reason to avoid those dates.
There is a small camping area and the hotel has rooms. Either is a better plan than trying to drive the whole highway and reach a town at the far end in one day.

sections.heading: Mount Taranaki is a serious mountain
body: The Pouākai Crossing and the summit route look approachable from the road and are not. Taranaki has a high fatality record, weather that changes within an hour, and terrain that becomes genuinely dangerous in cloud. It is not a mountain to attempt casually.

Check the forecast for the mountain rather than New Plymouth, tell someone your plan, and turn back early. The lower walks around Dawson Falls and the Kamahi loop give you the forest and the views without the exposure.
tips: Forecast the mountain, not the town
Taranaki weather turns within the hour
Lower walks give the views safely

sections.heading: New Plymouth is underrated as a base
body: The Coastal Walkway runs 13 kilometres along the waterfront, the Len Lye Centre is genuinely good, and the city has the services to reset a trip properly before or after the highway. It works far better as a two-night base than a single overnight.
Use it to do laundry, restock and check the mountain forecast before deciding which of the Egmont walks to attempt. The weather often makes that decision for you.

sections.heading: The Surf Highway and the coast
body: State Highway 45 loops around the western side of the mountain between New Plymouth and Hāwera, and it is a far easier drive than the Forgotten World Highway with a string of surf beaches along it. Ōakura, Ōpunake and Kina Beach all have camping and the coastline is consistently good.

The contrast is the point of a Taranaki loop: the mountain in the middle, forest and farmland on the eastern side, and a run of black sand surf beaches on the west. Doing both sides makes it a proper circuit rather than an out-and-back.

Cape Egmont lighthouse and the coastal road around Pungarehu give the classic view of the mountain rising straight out of farmland. It is best in the early morning before cloud forms on the summit, which it usually does by late morning.

sections.heading: Rail carts and the tunnel
body: Operators run rail carts along the disused Stratford to Okahukura line, including through the Hobbits Hole tunnel, which is a genuinely unusual way to see the country the highway passes through.
These need booking ahead and run to a schedule rather than on demand. If it appeals, build the day around the departure time rather than hoping to fit it in.
tips: Rail carts need booking ahead
Build the day around the departure

wellington-wairarapa-camping-loop.title: Wellington and Wairarapa: a 4-day camping loop
wellington-wairarapa-camping-loop.description: Harbour hills, vineyard towns and an exposed southern coast within a short circuit.
wellington-wairarapa-camping-loop.intro: Four days can move from Wellington's compact centre to Wairarapa wine country and the wild coast at Cape Palliser. The distances are moderate, but wind and the Remutaka road decide how relaxed they feel.

sections.heading: Cross the Remutaka Range
body: Leave Wellington after the commuter peak and take State Highway 2 toward Featherston. Strong wind, rain and traffic can make the crossing tiring in a high-sided campervan, so slow down or delay rather than fighting the vehicle.
Martinborough and Greytown make practical bases with food, powered sites and short local drives. If wine is part of the day, walk, cycle with care or use a tour instead of moving the vehicle.

sections.heading: Cape Palliser day
body: The road past Lake Ferry narrows and runs close to the sea before Cape Palliser. Check swell, wind and recent road conditions, then leave enough daylight for the return.
Keep distance from fur seals and never block the road or boat access around Ngawi. The lighthouse stairs are steep, and the coast offers little shelter when a southerly arrives.

sections.heading: Return through the towns
body: Use the final morning for the smaller Wairarapa towns or a walk around the wetlands, then cross the range before fatigue and evening traffic combine.
A Wellington-area holiday park can be the smartest last night before a ferry. It gives laundry, power and a predictable departure without adding a city-centre parking problem.

sections.heading: The Rimutaka Hill Road sets the tone
body: The road between Upper Hutt and Featherston climbs steeply with tight corners and is exposed to the wind that Wellington is known for. It is fine in a car and demands real attention in a campervan or with a trailer, particularly in a northerly.

Check the road status before crossing, because it closes to high-sided vehicles in strong wind and occasionally altogether. The alternative routes are long, so a closure changes the whole day rather than adding twenty minutes.
tips: Closes to high-sided vehicles in wind
Steep with tight corners
Detour routes are long

sections.heading: Cape Palliser is the best day on the loop
body: The drive out past Ngawi to the lighthouse takes you along an exposed coast lined with bulldozers used to launch fishing boats, past the largest fur seal colony on the North Island, to 250 steps up to the lighthouse. It feels considerably more remote than its distance from Wellington.
Keep well back from the seals, particularly between pups and the water, and never get between an animal and its escape route to the sea. They move faster than they look and will defend the space.

sections.heading: Martinborough works on a bicycle
body: The wineries sit in a compact grid within easy riding distance of the village square, which makes cycling between them the standard and sensible way to do a tasting day. Bike hire is available in the village and removes the drink-driving question entirely.
Book a table for lunch somewhere in advance on a weekend, because the village is small and fills. Most cellar doors charge a tasting fee that is credited against a purchase.
tips: Hire bikes, do not drive between wineries
Book weekend lunch ahead
Tasting fees credit against purchases

sections.heading: Wellington itself needs a plan for the vehicle
body: Parking a campervan in central Wellington is difficult and expensive, and the height restrictions catch people out in the central car parks. Base yourself in the Hutt Valley or at a coastal campground and use the train or bus into the city.
Te Papa is free and genuinely world class, and the cable car and Zealandia are both worth a half day. None of that requires the van to be anywhere near the centre.

sections.heading: Putangirua Pinnacles and the coast road
body: The Pinnacles are a badlands formation of eroded gravel spires reached by a walk up a streambed, and they were used as the Paths of the Dead in the film trilogy. The valley route is a scramble over loose rock; the ridge track above gives the overview and takes longer.

The road out to Cape Palliser beyond the Pinnacles is unsealed in places and can be affected by slips and by the sea in a big swell. Check conditions before committing, particularly in a large vehicle, because turning around is difficult.

Ngawi, the fishing village with a line of bulldozers on the beach, is the most photographed part of this coast and a good place to stop. There are no services beyond it, so fuel and food come from Martinborough or Featherston.

sections.heading: Zealandia and the city wildlife
body: Zealandia is a fenced urban sanctuary where kaka, takahe, tuatara and tui are common and visible, and the night tour offers a realistic chance of seeing kiwi close to the city centre.
It books out, particularly the night tour, and it is a much better wildlife experience than most people expect from something inside a capital city.
tips: Night tour offers a kiwi chance
Book the night tour ahead

north-island-two-week-road-trip.title: North Island camping road trip: a practical 14-day route
north-island-two-week-road-trip.description: Two weeks from Auckland through volcanic country, the capital and the western coast.
north-island-two-week-road-trip.imageAlt: Campervan route through the central North Island
north-island-two-week-road-trip.intro: A fortnight cannot cover every corner of Te Ika-a-Māui well. This route chooses a coherent loop, protects two-night stays in the places that need them and leaves Northland or East Cape for another journey.

sections.heading: Auckland to volcanic country
body: Spend the first night outside Auckland traffic, then give Coromandel and Rotorua two nights each. This creates time for a beach or forest day and a geothermal day without packing camp every morning.
Use Taupō to restock before Tongariro. Alpine plans must follow the forecast, transport arrangements and volcanic or track alerts, with a lower walk ready when conditions are wrong.

sections.heading: South to Wellington
body: Break the central drive around Whanganui or the Kāpiti Coast. Wellington rewards a parked vehicle, and a campground near public transport avoids height limits and expensive central parking.

If a Cook Strait ferry follows, check in according to the vehicle booking and allow for wind disruption. Keep medicines, warm layers and essential documents outside any vehicle deck you cannot access underway.

sections.heading: Return through Taranaki
body: Travel north through the Wairarapa only if time allows; otherwise use the west coast toward Taranaki. New Plymouth provides an easy two-night base for coast and mountain options.
Finish through Waikato with the final night close enough to Auckland for a calm return. Cleaning, fuel and rental handover take longer than the last line on the itinerary suggests.

sections.heading: Fourteen days means choosing a side
body: The common mistake is trying to include Northland, the Coromandel, the central plateau, the East Cape and Taranaki in one fortnight. That produces a driving holiday with no time in any of it. Pick either the northern loop or the eastern and central route and do it properly.

A workable shape is Auckland, Coromandel, Rotorua, Taupō, Tongariro, Napier, Wellington, with two nights in at least two of those. Northland then becomes a separate trip rather than a rushed appendage.
tips: Do not try to fit Northland in as well
Two nights in at least two places
Choose one loop and do it properly

sections.heading: Tongariro Alpine Crossing needs a real plan
body: It is a 19.4 kilometre one-way alpine route, requires shuttle transport at both ends, and there is a parking time limit at Mangatepopo that effectively forces the shuttle. It is also frequently closed or unsafe in wind, cloud or ice, and people get into serious trouble every year.

Book the shuttle, check the DOC forecast on the morning, carry warm and waterproof layers regardless of the sunshine at the car park, and be genuinely willing to abandon it. Leave a spare day in the itinerary so a cancellation is not the end of it.

sections.heading: Geothermal country rewards choosing carefully
body: Rotorua and Taupō have more geothermal attractions than anyone needs, and they are not interchangeable. Wai-O-Tapu, Waimangu, Orakei Korako and Craters of the Moon each offer something different and pricing varies widely, with one of them free.
Pick one paid park and one free thermal area rather than three paid ones. The novelty wears off faster than the entry fees suggest, and the money is better spent on a lake trip or a day walk.
tips: One paid park is usually enough
They are not interchangeable
Craters of the Moon is the cheap option

sections.heading: Leave the last day soft
body: If you are flying out of Auckland or catching a ferry from Wellington, do not plan to arrive on the morning of departure. Roadworks, weather and a slow last day are all normal, and the North Island's main routes carry heavy traffic around holidays.
Spend the final night within an hour of the terminal or airport. It converts a stressful morning into an ordinary one and costs nothing more than a slightly duller last campsite.

sections.heading: Waitomo, Napier and the stops that get cut
body: Waitomo's glowworm caves are a genuine highlight and sit awkwardly between Auckland and the central plateau, which is why they often get dropped. The black water rafting is more memorable than the standard walking tour if you have the time and inclination.

Napier's art deco centre is compact enough to see in a morning and pairs well with the Hawke's Bay wineries, most of which are within cycling distance of the city. It works best as a two-night stop rather than a pass-through.
If the fortnight is tight, Napier is the more defensible cut, because Waitomo has no substitute anywhere else on the route while wine regions appear again in Marlborough if you continue south.

sections.heading: Where the driving days bite
body: Auckland to the Coromandel, and Taupo to Napier over the Titiokura, are the two legs most often underestimated. Both include winding sections that stretch well past their routing estimate.
Break either one with a stop rather than treating it as a transit. The alternative is arriving somewhere good with no energy left to enjoy it.
tips: Auckland to Coromandel runs long
Taupo to Napier is winding

picton-kaikoura-christchurch-route.title: Picton to Christchurch via Kaikōura: a 4-day coastal route
picton-kaikoura-christchurch-route.description: Sounds, vineyards, marine wildlife and a mountain-backed highway down the east coast.
picton-kaikoura-christchurch-route.imageAlt: Kaikōura coast with mountains behind the road
picton-kaikoura-christchurch-route.intro: The direct drive is short enough for one day, but four days reveals a far richer coast. The plan gives Picton time to settle after the ferry, Kaikōura a full weather window and North Canterbury a final unhurried stop.

sections.heading: Picton and Marlborough
body: Do not rush straight from a late ferry onto the coastal highway. Use Picton for the first night, then explore the Sounds or travel through Blenheim after a proper rest.
Cellar doors require a sober driving plan and many operate by booking or seasonal hours. A campsite near Blenheim or Renwick lets the vehicle stay put while a tour handles transport.

sections.heading: Two nights in Kaikōura
body: State Highway 1 is exposed to weather, slips and occasional closures. Check the route before leaving Marlborough, then use the coastal pull-offs only where stopping is clearly safe.
Whale trips depend on sea conditions and may move or cancel. Two nights create a second opportunity, while the peninsula walkway, seal viewing and local food keep the spare day valuable.

sections.heading: North Canterbury finish
body: Waipara offers a slower break before Christchurch, with beaches and small towns nearby. Keep the final day light if city driving in a large vehicle is unfamiliar.
Choose a Christchurch campground based on the next task: airport, rental depot, city visit or inland departure. The best site is the one that removes an unnecessary crossing of the city.

sections.heading: The coast road has been rebuilt and still moves
body: State Highway 1 between Picton and Christchurch was severely damaged in the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake and has been substantially rebuilt, but the coastal section remains prone to slips and closures in heavy rain. Check the NZTA status before committing to it rather than assuming it is open.
When it closes, the inland route via the Lewis Pass is the alternative and adds several hours. That is worth knowing before you book something time-critical at either end.
tips: Check NZTA before the coast road
Slips still close it in heavy rain
Lewis Pass detour adds hours

sections.heading: Kaikōura is a booking, not a drive-through
body: Whale watching, dolphin swimming and albatross trips all run to weather and all book out in season. The whales are resident year-round, which makes Kaikōura unusually reliable, but the sea state cancels trips regularly enough that a single-night stop is a gamble.
Stay two nights and book the trip for the first morning. That gives the operator a second window to reschedule you into rather than refunding you as you drive away.

sections.heading: The seal colony and the peninsula walk
body: The colony at Point Kean is free, accessible and busy with fur seals, and the peninsula walkway above it is one of the better short coastal walks in the country. Keep twenty metres back from the animals and never block their path to the water.
The walkway is tide-dependent on the shore route and unaffected on the clifftop route. Check the tide before choosing which way round, or you will be turning back.
tips: Twenty metres from the seals
Shore route is tide-dependent
Clifftop route always works

sections.heading: Blenheim and the Waipara wineries
body: Marlborough around Blenheim is the country's largest wine region and most cellar doors are within a compact area, which makes a bicycle the sensible way to visit several. Waipara, closer to Christchurch, is smaller, quieter and often more interesting for a single stop.
If the itinerary only allows one wine stop, Waipara fits the route better on this drive and does not require a detour off the highway. Marlborough deserves its own day rather than a rushed afternoon.

sections.heading: Queen Charlotte Drive and the Sounds
body: The road from Picton to Havelock is only 35 kilometres and takes the better part of an hour, with continuous corners, narrow sections and viewpoints worth stopping at. It is the better alternative to the direct highway if you have the time, and a poor choice at dusk when tired.

Anakiwa at the end of the Queen Charlotte Track and the campsites around Momorangi Bay put you on the water and make a good first South Island night. Water taxis from Picton open up the walking track without committing to the full multi-day route.
If you are arriving on an evening sailing, stay in Picton rather than attempting this road in the dark. It is the kind of route where the scenery is the entire reason to take it.

sections.heading: Where to break the drive
body: Picton to Christchurch is comfortably done in two days with a night in Kaikoura, and uncomfortably in one. The direct run is around five hours before any stops, on a road with plenty worth stopping for.
Waipara and the Hurunui are the natural second break if you have three days, with wineries and the Hanmer Springs detour inland.
tips: Two days beats one
Hanmer Springs is an easy detour

christchurch-tekapo-aoraki-road-trip.title: Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and Aoraki: a 5-day road trip
christchurch-tekapo-aoraki-road-trip.description: Canterbury plains, turquoise lakes and alpine weather on the classic inland route.
christchurch-tekapo-aoraki-road-trip.imageAlt: Road toward Aoraki beside Lake Pūkaki
christchurch-tekapo-aoraki-road-trip.intro: Five days lets the Mackenzie Basin breathe. The journey is strongest when Tekapo and Aoraki each get a full day, with the weather deciding which walks and viewpoints belong on the schedule.

sections.heading: Cross the Canterbury Plains
body: Buy specialist food, fuel and equipment in Christchurch, then use Geraldine for a relaxed first break. Strong nor'west winds can affect high-sided vehicles even before the mountains appear.
Lake Tekapo fills quickly in peak seasons. Book the legal overnight stop instead of assuming an empty lakeside area permits camping, and protect the dark-sky environment by keeping light low.

sections.heading: Tekapo to Aoraki
body: Follow Lake Pūkaki north only after checking the Aoraki road and park alerts. The view encourages frequent stops, but use formed pull-offs and leave traffic lanes clear.
Aoraki weather changes rapidly and popular walks can close for wind, avalanche or flood risk. Start early, carry layers and choose a short valley walk when the alpine forecast turns.

sections.heading: Twizel and the return
body: Twizel provides fuel, groceries and a sheltered alternative to the exposed upper valley. It is also a sensible place to add a recovery night after a long hike.
Return through Fairlie or continue toward Wānaka only with a realistic driving day. The scenery does not make fatigue, crosswind or rental return times less real.

sections.heading: The Mackenzie is a dark sky reserve
body: The Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve covers Tekapo, Twizel and the Aoraki area, and the night sky here is among the best accessible anywhere. Lighting is restricted throughout the reserve, which is why the stars are as good as they are.
Use a red torch, keep vehicle headlights off where you can, and give your eyes twenty minutes to adapt properly. A phone screen at full brightness undoes that for everyone around you.
tips: Use a red torch at night
Twenty minutes for eyes to adapt
Lighting is restricted for a reason

sections.heading: Tekapo is beautiful and extremely busy
body: The Church of the Good Shepherd is one of the most photographed buildings in the country and the coach traffic reflects that. Early morning and late evening are the only times it feels like the place in the photographs.

It is also an active church rather than a monument, and services take priority over photography. The lupins along the lakeshore, incidentally, are an invasive weed rather than a native feature, however good they look in November.

sections.heading: Aoraki weather and the Hooker Valley
body: The Hooker Valley Track is the standout short walk in the park: three hours return, largely flat, three swing bridges and a glacial lake at the end with the mountain above it. It is achievable for most people and worth timing for early light.

The weather at the village is not the weather in the valley, and wind funnels hard through it. Take a windproof layer even on a warm day, and check the forecast at the visitor centre rather than relying on a town forecast from Twizel.
tips: Hooker Valley is three hours return
Wind funnels hard through the valley
Check forecasts at the visitor centre

sections.heading: Accommodation is concentrated and books out
body: Aoraki village has limited beds and the DOC campsite at White Horse Hill fills daily in summer. Twizel and Lake Pukaki have more options and are within reasonable driving distance, which makes them the practical base for most travellers.
Book ahead in summer without exception, and note that there is no supermarket at the village. Restock in Twizel or Fairlie before heading up the valley.

sections.heading: Geraldine, Fairlie and the approach
body: The inland route through Geraldine and Fairlie is the standard approach and both towns are worth a stop for supplies, with Fairlie being the last practical restock before Tekapo. The climb over Burkes Pass marks the transition into the Mackenzie and the change in landscape is abrupt.

Lake Pukaki's viewpoint on the way to Aoraki gives the classic view up the lake to the mountain, and the colour is genuinely as unnatural as the photographs suggest, caused by suspended glacial flour. Early morning is calmest and the reflections are best before the wind gets up.

The road into Aoraki village is a dead end, 55 kilometres each way from the highway. Factor the return into the day rather than treating it as a stop on the way somewhere, because there is no through route.

sections.heading: Hot pools and the wet-day option
body: Tekapo Springs and the pools at Omarama give you something to do when the weather closes in, which in the Mackenzie it does with little warning. Both are within easy reach of the main route.
The Mount John observatory tours are weather dependent and book out. If the forecast is clear on your first night, take it then rather than saving it.
tips: Take a clear night when you get it
Hot pools cover a bad weather day

west-coast-south-island-road-trip.title: South Island West Coast camping road trip
west-coast-south-island-road-trip.description: Rainforest, limestone, glaciers and the Tasman Sea from Westport to Haast.
west-coast-south-island-road-trip.imageAlt: Rainforest meeting the Tasman Sea on the West Coast
west-coast-south-island-road-trip.intro: The West Coast is a journey through weather rather than a checklist of sights. Six or seven days gives rain room to move, keeps glacier valleys from becoming rushed stops and places every long section inside daylight.

sections.heading: Westport to Hokitika
body: Check the Buller Gorge and coastal highway before leaving, then pause at Punakaiki around the tide and swell rather than a fixed minute. Blowholes are natural features, not scheduled performances.
Hokitika is the first strong resupply and a good place to dry gear. Buy pounamu only from reputable local sellers and treat cultural stories with more care than a souvenir label.

sections.heading: Glacier country
body: Franz Josef and Fox offer valley walks, weather-dependent flights and busy holiday accommodation. Current glacier access follows marked tracks and closures; old photos do not indicate where visitors can safely stand today.
Keep one unbooked activity window because cloud and rain move quickly. A wet day can still suit forest walks, hot pools or a slow drive, but never cross a barrier for a clearer view.

sections.heading: Haast and the alpine exit
body: The road south includes narrow bridges, waterfalls and sandfly country. Carry repellent, close screens early and use designated pull-offs instead of stopping on bends.
Before crossing Haast Pass, check for snow, slips and closures. Fuel in Haast or Fox and reach Wānaka before dark, because the final lakeside bends demand full attention.

sections.heading: Rain is the condition, not the exception
body: Parts of the West Coast receive over five metres of rain a year, and Fox and Franz Josef sit in some of the wettest inhabited country anywhere. A trip planned around avoiding rain here will fail; a trip planned around travelling in it works fine.

Pack for it properly: a genuinely waterproof shell, dry bags for everything that matters, spare socks, and somewhere in the vehicle to dry things. The reward is near-empty campsites and rainforest that looks the way it does because of the weather.
tips: Plan to travel in rain, not avoid it
Dry bags for anything that matters
Empty campsites are the payoff

sections.heading: The sandflies are not an exaggeration
body: West Coast sandflies are relentless at dawn and dusk, near water, and in still conditions. They will find any gap in the tent mesh and the bites itch for days. This single factor ruins more West Coast trips than the rain does.

Carry strong repellent and apply it before you get out of the vehicle rather than after. Cover ankles and wrists in the evening, check the tent mesh before you leave home, and pack antihistamine cream because you will want it.

sections.heading: The glaciers have retreated a long way
body: Franz Josef and Fox no longer have valley-floor access to the ice, and the terminal face is well beyond where the walking tracks end. The valley walks are still worth doing, but the only way onto the ice is a helicopter, which is expensive and weather-dependent.

Book a heli-hike early in your stay so a weather cancellation can be rescheduled. If it does not run, the Franz Josef valley walk and the Fox glacier viewpoint still give you the scale, and the Lake Matheson reflection walk is arguably the better experience.
tips: No valley-floor ice access any more
Heli-hikes cancel often for weather
Lake Matheson is the reliable alternative

sections.heading: Fuel, food and the Haast gap
body: The coast has long stretches between services, and the section from Fox through Haast to Wānaka is the one to plan for. Fill up before Haast, carry food, and expect no reception through much of it.

Punakaiki, Hokitika and Greymouth all have supplies and are worth stops in their own right. The pancake rocks are best at high tide with a swell running, which is worth checking rather than arriving at slack water on a calm day.

sections.heading: Punakaiki, Hokitika and the stops between
body: The Pancake Rocks at Punakaiki are best at high tide with a westerly swell running, when the blowholes work. At low tide on a calm day they are still interesting but considerably less dramatic, so check the tide before deciding when to stop.

Hokitika Gorge, about half an hour inland from the town, has water of a turquoise colour that looks manipulated in photographs and is not. It is a short easy walk and one of the better value stops on the coast.

Between the towns, the coast has a string of DOC sites and lagoons that reward an unplanned stop. Lake Mahinapua, Lake Ianthe and Ship Creek all have short walks and are far quieter than the glacier villages.

sections.heading: Whitebait, greenstone and local rules
body: Whitebait season runs in spring with strict rules on method and location, and it is taken very seriously locally. Pounamu is legally owned by Ngai Tahu and taking greenstone from rivers and beaches is not permitted.
Buy pounamu from a licensed carver instead, which supports the people it belongs to and gets you a better piece than a river pebble.
tips: Do not take greenstone from rivers
Buy pounamu from a licensed carver

queenstown-glenorchy-camping.title: Queenstown to Glenorchy: a 3-day camping escape
queenstown-glenorchy-camping.description: A short road with enough lake, mountain and walking country to fill a long weekend.
queenstown-glenorchy-camping.intro: The road to Glenorchy is only about 46 kilometres, but it deserves a full day. Three nights allow Queenstown supplies, a legal lakeside camp and one weather-dependent walk without turning every viewpoint into a hurried stop.

sections.heading: Leave Queenstown prepared
body: Fuel and shop before leaving town, then confirm the selected campground and its vehicle limits. Twelve Mile Delta is exposed and basic, while commercial options provide more certainty for power and showers.
Pull over only in formed bays on the Glenorchy road. Traffic, cyclists and blind corners make an improvised photo stop dangerous even when the lake appears empty.

sections.heading: Glenorchy day
body: Walk the lagoon boardwalk, visit the waterfront and choose a track that matches the forecast. Rees-Dart, Routeburn and Greenstone access involve different roads, bridges and backcountry preparation.
Glenorchy services are smaller than Queenstown's. Do not arrive expecting late fuel, groceries or an immediate mechanical repair, and carry cash or an alternative payment method.

sections.heading: Paradise or a slow return
body: Roads beyond Glenorchy can be unsealed, narrow and affected by fords or washouts. Rental conditions may prohibit the route, so stop where the vehicle agreement and current conditions stop.
Return with daylight and use Bob's Cove or another formed stop for the final walk. Let the lake road remain the experience instead of squeezing it between Queenstown bookings.

sections.heading: The Glenorchy road is the attraction
body: The 45 kilometres from Queenstown along the lake is one of the great drives in the country, with a series of signed viewpoints that are all worth stopping at. Bennett's Bluff in particular deserves more than a slow drive past.
